title: Port of Claim
description: A negotiation adventure about trade, law and succession at the moment a new port is being planned.
learningObjectives: Explain why the East India Company wanted a port at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
Describe the disputed Johor succession and why Raffles recognised Tengku Hussein.
Evaluate the risks each stakeholder took in signing the 1819 agreements.

player.name: The Interpreter
player.role: Junior interpreter attached to Raffles' expedition
player.brief: You translate, carry notes and help compare what each side is really agreeing to.

sharedContext.text: You travel with Raffles's small expedition. British merchants want a safe harbour at the southern end of the Straits, but Raffles must avoid a clash with the Dutch. Singapore looks useful, yet the Temenggong is not the Sultan and the Johor throne is disputed. Your job is to listen closely and help decide what kind of agreement can stand.

spans.quote: they had no safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
to establish a post at the southern end of the Straits but to avoid any collision with the Dutch
only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.
And the Johor throne itself was disputed.

assumptions.text: Raffles's private tone, hidden worries and limits of knowledge are inferred from his actions and orders.
assumptions.rationale: The sources show what he argued and did, but not his full inner thoughts.

assumptions.text: The Temenggong's private calculations are inferred from his authority on the island and his later decision to send for Hussein.
assumptions.rationale: The sources record his position and actions, but not a personal statement of motives.

assumptions.text: Hussein's private hopes and doubts are inferred from his disputed claim, his obscurity in Riau and the payments offered in the treaty.
assumptions.rationale: The sources do not preserve his personal speech in these meetings.

assumptions.text: Farquhar's private outlook is inferred from the role he was meant to take in the new settlement.
assumptions.rationale: The sources show his formal position, but not his personal views during the negotiations.

sharedContext.text: The first agreement is not enough. The throne of Johor is disputed. Hussein is the elder son, but he was away when his father died. His younger brother was installed and later recognised by the Dutch. Now Hussein has been brought to Singapore.

spans.quote: And the Johor throne itself was disputed.
The elder, Tengku Hussein, also known as Tengku Long, was away in Pahang for his wedding when his father died.
The younger, Tengku Abdul Rahman, was installed as Sultan in his absence
and this choice was later recognised by the Dutch.
Hussein arrived in Singapore in early February 1819

decision.prompt: The paper is ready. Signing now could secure the port Raffles wants, but it rests on a disputed succession and may trigger Dutch protest. Do you urge the parties to sign, to narrow the arrangement, or to stop until the claim is less risky?

endings.title: Missed Window
endings.summary: You hold the expedition back before any written opening is made. The chance for a quick foothold on Singapore slips away, and the mission leaves without turning local talks into a formal step.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, Raffles and the Temenggong did sign a preliminary agreement on 30 January 1819. Then Hussein arrived, and on 6 February a treaty was signed that allowed the Company to establish a trading post at Singapore.

spans.quote: On 30 January 1819 Raffles and the Temenggong signed a preliminary agreement
Hussein arrived in Singapore in early February 1819
On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed
The Company was permitted to establish a factory, or trading post, at Singapore.

endings.divergence: This ending differs from the record because the real expedition secured a preliminary agreement first and then moved on to a treaty.
reflectionQuestions: Why might speed matter in a contest over ports and sea lanes?
Was legal certainty more important than getting a first foothold?
Who gained the most from turning talk into a written agreement quickly?

endings.title: Legal Deadlock
endings.summary: You advise against recognising Hussein or against signing while the claim is disputed. The British avoid a risky move, but they also fail to secure a lawful local grant in time.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, Raffles recognised Hussein as Sultan Hussein Shah of Johor. A treaty was then signed between the Company, Hussein and the Temenggong on 6 February 1819.

spans.quote: Raffles recognised him as Sultan Hussein Shah of Johor.
On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.

endings.divergence: This ending differs from the record because the real negotiations broke the deadlock by recognising Hussein and using that recognition to sign.
reflectionQuestions: Why did Raffles think Hussein's claim was useful as well as lawful?
What risks came from choosing one claimant over another?
Could refusing to choose a side also be a political choice?

endings.title: Treaty Signed at Singapore
endings.summary: You help carry the negotiations to a full signature. The Company gains its post, Hussein is recognised, the Temenggong is included, and Farquhar is set to remain and run the settlement.

historicalOutcome.text: This ending matches the record. On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed. The Company was permitted to establish a trading post at Singapore, yearly payments were promised to Hussein and the Temenggong, and Raffles appointed Farquhar as Resident and Commandant.

endings.title: A Weaker Arrangement
endings.summary: You steer the talks toward a narrower, temporary deal. A British foothold may still appear, but its legal basis is thinner and every side leaves with more doubt about what has really been secured.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, the agreement was not left vague. On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed that permitted a trading post at Singapore, set yearly payments, and was followed by Farquhar's appointment.
